newsitem.title: USA: Colombia pleads with U.S. to back it in drugs war.
newsitem.headline: Colombia pleads with U.S. to back it in drugs war.

text.p: Colombia's vice-president urged the United States on Thursday to reinstate his country as an ally in the anti-drug war, saying punitive measures would only drive people into the arms of drug traffickers and guerrillas.
Carlos Lemos Simmonds said any economic sanctions would hit trade and investment and create hardships that would hinder, not help, the battle against Colombia's drug lords.

"It would be dangerous for the U.S. government to act in a way that helps create uncertainty and instability in Latin America's oldest democracy," he told a forum organised by U.S. and Latin American businessmen in Miami to back Colombia's case for recertification as a drugs war ally.
Washington last year denied certification to Colombia, whose drugs lords dominate the international cocaine trade, saying it was not doing enough to tackle the problem.

President Bill Clinton will announce his decision on recertification on March 1. If Colombia stays on the black list -- as U.S. sources say is likely -- it could face economic sanctions and cuts in aid.

Simmonds protested that Colombian security forces and government officials had made great progress in the past two years, arresting drugs cartel leaders, smashing refineries and plantations and seizing helicopters and weapons arsenals.

"A first effect of decertification would be to hurt people who are not part of the problem but rather provide alternatives to it," he said. "A growing and prosperous Colombia is one of the best ways to fight drug trafficking."

Sanctions would lead to job losses and social unrestm he added. "Tragically some of those newly unemployed Colombians might decide in their desperation that the only solution to their financial troubles would be dedicating their time to the dangerous and corrupt but lucrative business of growing crops for and or trafficking in the business of illicit drugs."

Bogota has the backing of powerful Hispanic business groups in Miami, a hub of more than $14 billion worth of bilateral trade and investment. Saying U.S. jobs and business, particulalry in south Florida, also stand to suffer, they have formed the Coalition to Certify Colombia to plan a strategy to convince Washington to change its mind.

Alfredo Quintero, president of Miami's Colombian-American Chamber of Commerce, said he was not confident they would succeed. "Colombia is a scapegoat for the State Department," he told Reuters. "The only thing I am hoping for is that we don't receive sanctions. That would be very unfair to banks and businesses who are working honestly."
Colombia's government also seemed resigned to another year on the black list. Rafael Lamos, under-secretary in the presidency, said it was becoming apparent that Colombia would not be recertified.

U.S. drug fighters were enraged last month when a judge in Cali handed down five-year jail sentences to Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, brothers who head the notorious Cali cocaine cartel. Much tougher sentences had been demanded.
Legislation is still pending before Colombia's Congress on stiffer penalties for drug traffickers.
